name: MAC Montréal
overview: Museum of contemporary art founded by the Quebec government in 1964, described as the first institution in Canada devoted exclusively to contemporary art (Wikipedia).
Its building at Place des Arts opened on 28 May 1992 in the Quartier des spectacles. Jodoin Lamarre Pratte & Associés won the 1983 to 1984 architecture competition (Wikipedia).
Its earlier homes were Place Ville-Marie (1964 to 1965), Château Dufresne (1965 to 1968) and a gallery at Cité du Havre from 1968 to 1992 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: MAC Montréal: mainly public: Quebec government crown corporation, with private donors through the MAC Foundation
wider_context: On 18 December 2019 SNC-Lavalin's construction division pleaded guilty to one count of fraud over 5,000 dollars over its work in Libya, with a 280 million dollar penalty and three years' probation; the remaining charges, which alleged payments of nearly 48 million dollars to public officials under the Gaddafi regime from 2001 to 2011, were stayed (The Canadian Press, "SNC-Lavalin pleads guilty to fraud, will pay a $280M fine for Libyan work", 18 December 2019). Wikipedia names the convicted company as SNC-Lavalin Construction Inc.

Wikipedia states that SNC-Lavalin is now named AtkinsRéalis. AtkinsRéalis Canada inc. is a donor to the MAC Foundation in the 2024-25 donor list and a governor partner of the Foundation's 2024 gala (2024-25 annual report).

name: PHI Foundation
overview: Not-for-profit contemporary art foundation in Old Montréal, with exhibitions at 451 rue Saint-Jean and 407 rue Saint-Pierre (phi.ca).
Founded by Phoebe Greenberg, who was inspired by the Fondation Cartier. It opened on 5 October 2007 as DHC/ART at 451 rue Saint-Jean (phi.ca; Canadian Art, Leah Sandals, 2017).
Renamed PHI Foundation for Contemporary Art in 2019 (phi.ca).
funding_verdict: PHI Foundation: mainly private: Phoebe Greenberg's family wealth, with public money for the expansion

press_items.title: Sky Goodden, "The Seductive Branding of Phoebe Greenberg" (2019)
Kate Taylor, "Montreal's Phi Foundation wants to make art an urban routine" (2022)

name: Oakville Galleries
overview: A not-for-profit contemporary art museum (HIP directory, updated 14 July 2026): one institution with two buildings and an 11-acre garden fronting Lake Ontario, at Centennial Square, 120 Navy Street, and Gairloch Gardens, 1306 Lakeshore Road East. It focuses on the presentation, collection, preservation and interpretation of recent work in the visual and media arts (Visit Oakville).

Gairloch Gardens: Colonel W.G. MacKendrick had the house built in 1923 to 1924. Toronto investment banker James Gairdner bought the estate, named it Gairloch, and on his death in 1972 left it to the Town of Oakville for use as a park and gallery. The town designated the property under the Ontario Heritage Act in 1986 (Canada's Historic Places).
A registered charity, number 119064418RR0001 (gallery website).
funding_verdict: Oakville Galleries: mixed: public arts funders and the Town of Oakville, with corporate sponsors, foundations and individual donors
wider_context: Siemens: in January 2020, after protests, the company said it would carry out its contract to supply rail signalling for Adani's Carmichael coal mine in Queensland. Chief executive Joe Kaeser wrote in an open letter that there was no legally and economically responsible way to unwind the contract (Mining Technology, Matthew Hall, "Siemens to pursue Adani mine contract despite pressure from protesters", 13 January 2020). Wikipedia gives the contract value as $20 million and adds that Greta Thunberg called on Siemens to stop delivering equipment.
The gallery's Funding & Partners page shows Siemens under Gold Sponsor. The protests targeted Siemens, not Oakville Galleries.

name: Art Metropole
overview: Non-profit artist-run centre and bookshop at 896 College Street, Toronto, that publishes, promotes, exhibits, archives and distributes artists' books, multiples and related media (Art Metropole website).

Founded in 1974 by the artist collective General Idea as a division of Art-Official Inc. (established 1972), the non-profit publisher of File Megazine (1972 to 1989) (Art Metropole website). It opened first in "an abandoned space over a Greek restaurant in downtown Toronto" (Wikipedia).
The site calls the shop the oldest and longest-running artist-run bookstore in the world.
funding_verdict: Art Metropole: mainly public arts funding: Canada Council for the Arts, Ontario Arts Council and Toronto Arts Council

name: YYZ Artists' Outlet
overview: Artist-run exhibition space and publisher at #140-401 Richmond St. W, Toronto. Its mission is to "offer the space for our community to show, share, and grow" (stated by YYZ).

Founded in 1979 by graduates of the Ontario College of Art and Design, who staged their first show at 567 Queen Street West (stated by YYZ). The Community Stories project says several Toronto artists founded it as an artist-run centre.
YYZ says it started on Queen Street, moved to Spadina and has been at 401 Richmond since 1997.
funding_verdict: YYZ Artists' Outlet: public grants and donations: Ontario Arts Council operating grants, the Ontario Trillium Foundation and private donors

name: Arthur Erickson House and Garden
overview: Garden and former home of the architect Arthur Erickson at 4195 West 14th Avenue in Point Grey, Vancouver. The Foundation's office is separate, at 410 to 1639 West 2nd Avenue (iconichouses.org, aefoundation.ca).

A house built in 1924 that Erickson lived in for 52 years, until just before his death on 20 May 2009. The Foundation dates his stay from 1957, Heritage Site Finder dates his purchase to 1954 (aefoundation.ca, heritagesitefinder.ca).
Named for Erickson, who once said the house was built as a garage and small living space for a family that never built a larger home (Heritage Site Finder).
funding_verdict: Arthur Erickson House and Garden: charity-funded: tour fees, memberships and donations, with a small federal grant

name: Artspeak
overview: Non-profit, artist-run gallery and publisher at 233 Carrall Street in Gastown, Vancouver, registered as the I.E. Artspeak Gallery Society (CanadaHelps).

Founded in 1986 at the Kootenay School of Writing, a writers' collective in Vancouver, by Jeff Derksen, Cate Rimmer and the artist Kay Higgins. Rimmer and Higgins ran it as volunteers at first (Wikipedia). It became independent in 1987 and moved to 311 West Hastings (Wikipedia).
In 1996 it bought its present building at 233 Carrall Street. Wikipedia says it is one of the few artist-run centres in Vancouver to own its space.
funding_verdict: Artspeak: public arts grants and donations: BC Arts Council grants, plus fundraisers

name: Western Front
overview: Non-profit artist-run centre at 303 E 8th Ave in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood of Vancouver.

Founded in 1973 by Kate Craig, Glenn Lewis, Eric Metcalfe, Michael Morris, Vincent Trasov, Martin Bartlett, Mo van Nostrand and Henry Greenhow as a shared place to live and work. Registered as a non-profit society in 1974 (the centre's about page).
Named for the building's pioneer-style facade, its West Coast location and the founders' avant-garde pursuits, according to the centre's own history page.
funding_verdict: Western Front: mainly public grants, with a founders' endowment society and private donors

press_items.title: Tessa Vikander, "Western Front Society set to purchase its historic space" (2016)

name: grunt gallery
overview: Artist-run centre in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood of Vancouver, British Columbia, at 116-350 East 2nd Avenue (grunt website, Wikipedia).

Founded in 1984 by eight artists: Hillary Wood, Dawn Richards, Kempton Dexter, Glenn Alteen, spike mckinley, Danielle Peacock, Billy Gene Wallace and Garry Ross. Ross designed the logo (grunt website).
Wikipedia says the first meetings for the Vancouver Fringe Festival took place at grunt in 1985, and that a weekly jazz improvisation series, Jazz in the Gallery, ran from 1987 to 1994.
funding_verdict: grunt gallery: mainly public: federal, provincial and city arts funding, with foundations, donors and a capital grant for its building

name: Audain Art Museum
overview: Private museum of British Columbia art at 4350 Blackcomb Way in Whistler, on the "unceded, shared territory" of the Squamish and Lil'wat Nations (stated by the museum).

Founded by Michael Audain and Yoshiko Karasawa to house British Columbia works from their private collection. Audain chose the site in September 2012 and agreed with the Resort Municipality of Whistler in December 2012 to build. Construction began in August 2013 and the museum opened in March 2016 (stated by the museum).
Named for Michael Audain, who is chairman and major shareholder of the home builder Polygon Homes (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Audain Art Museum: self-funded: the founders' collection and foundation, with an endowment and donations

press_items.title: Marsha Lederman, "How a $100-million private donation put the Vancouver Art Gallery's transformation back on track" (2022)
"2017 AZ Awards Winner: Architecture Over 1,000 Square Metres" (2017)

name: Plug In ICA
overview: Contemporary art institute at Unit 1, 460 Portage Avenue, Winnipeg, in the Buhler Centre at Memorial Boulevard and Colony Street, a building it shares with the University of Winnipeg (plugin.org; The Manitoban, 2012).

Established in 1972 as a not-for-profit exhibition space run by a board of practising artists. Lorraine Raboud and Suzanne Gillies were the founding directors (plugin.org/history; The Manitoban). It started in a loft at 90 Albert Street and later moved to 175 McDermot Street, with earlier addresses on Arthur and Donald Streets (The Manitoban).
Earlier name: Plug In. Plugin.org says a survey of ICA models in the UK and US found its mission fits "most comfortably within the ICA model," and it does not state a formal designation.
funding_verdict: Plug In ICA: mainly public: federal government grants, with private donors, sponsors and a gala

press_items.title: Leah Hansen, "40 years strong for Plug In" (2012)

name: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos
overview: Museum at Avenida Matucana 501, Santiago, on the human rights violations of the military dictatorship of 1973 to 1990 (Spanish Wikipedia).
President Michelle Bachelet laid the first stone on 10 December 2008 and inaugurated the museum on 11 January 2010 (Spanish Wikipedia).
Not named for a person.
funding_verdict: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos: mainly public: Government of Chile, through the national heritage service, paid to a private-law foundation that runs the museum

press_items.title: newsroom desk, "Senado revierte negativa de la Cámara y repone recursos para instituciones de DD.HH." (2022)
Leonardo Casas, "Museo de la Memoria tiene área sobre atentado a Pinochet" (2018)

name: CRAC Valparaíso (Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo)
aliases: Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo
overview: Collaborative non-profit platform for socio-artistic productions across the city of Valparaíso, with offices at Avenida Prat 798, oficina 574 (stated by the space in its TransArtists listing).
An independent project with a flexible, autonomous management model, running since 2007 (stated by the space; TransArtists and Dutch Art Institute listings).

It runs residencies for artists and researchers as city practices: residents hold talks, workshops, performances and seminars with the local community, which feed the centre's archive (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: CRAC Valparaíso: self-sustained non-profit, as stated by the space

name: Red Brick Art Museum
overview: Private contemporary art museum in the No. 1 International Art District (一号地国际艺术区), Cuigezhuang, in north-east Chaoyang District, Beijing (Visit Beijing; Our China Story; Beijing municipal government).

Founded by the collector and entrepreneur Yan Shijie (闫士杰, also written 阎士杰) and his wife Cao Mei; planning began in 2007 and the museum opened in May 2014 (Our China Story, Chinese edition; Beijing municipal government).
Dezeen describes it as a folk-based, non-profit art museum showing Chinese and world art (Dezeen, 2017).
funding_verdict: Red Brick Art Museum: self-funded: the founding couple's private money
wider_context: 2017 protest at an opening: Liu Yukuan (刘彧宽), the museum's public relations manager, died suddenly on 30 December 2016. On 27 May 2017 his parents came to an exhibition opening holding his portrait and handing out leaflets; more than ten museum staff dragged them away and forced them into two cars (The Paper, Gu Yizhi, June 2017).
Unverified: the family said the museum owed Liu his last month's wages and that he died of overwork; the museum called the wage claim false.
The museum's statement admitted that "lack of experience" (经验不足) in handling the day had hurt Liu's parents' feelings and apologised (The Paper, our translation).
The parents had bruises and abrasions on their hands and bodies; the dispute had not been settled when The Paper wrote.
The protest was aimed at the museum itself, by a former employee's family.

press_items.title: Gu Yizhi (顾一指), "开幕式成'打戏'，美术馆建设的'道'依然崎岖" ("The opening becomes a brawl; the road of museum building is still rough", our translation) (2017)

name: Rockbund Art Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum at 20 Huqiu Road, Huangpu District, Shanghai (museum website), on the northern tip of the Bund area (Institute of Network Cultures). The nearest Metro station is East Nanjing Road, on Lines 2 and 10 (Wikipedia).

Opened in 2010 as part of the Rockbund Urban Renaissance project to renovate heritage buildings at the north end of the Bund (DutchCulture). Geert Lovink dates the opening to May 2010, timed with the Shanghai World Expo (Institute of Network Cultures).

The museum occupies the former Royal Asiatic Society building, completed in 1933 and designed by Palmer and Turner. The same building housed one of China's first modern museums, the earlier Shanghai Museum (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Rockbund Art Museum: founders Lynn and Thomas Ou, with lead sponsors ROCKBUND and Ping An

press_items.title: Geert Lovink, "Cia Guo-Qiang's Romantic Resolution of the Peasant Question" (18 July 2010; title as published)

name: TANK Shanghai
overview: Private art museum and 60,000-square-metre art park on the West Bund waterfront of the Huangpu River, Xuhui District, at Longteng Avenue (Time Out gives 2350, the Chinese Art Foundations page gives 2380).

Founded by the collector Qiao Zhibing, a karaoke club owner, who planned it for more than four years and was invited to create it by the government-backed West Bund Development Group. It opened on 23 March 2019 after a delay from November 2018 (The Art Newspaper, Lisa Movius, 22 March 2019).

Building: five decommissioned aviation fuel tanks from the historic 1917 Longhua Airport, converted by Beijing-based OPEN Architecture. The Art Newspaper puts the buildings at roughly 10,000 square metres, about 60 percent exhibition space. Three tanks are linked by a new building and two freestanding tanks serve as a clubhouse and event space.
funding_verdict: TANK Shanghai: founder-funded with a state-backed partner: Qiao Zhibing's money, with the West Bund Group inviting him and managing the park
wider_context: ArtAsiaPacific, Mioie Kwok, "Shanghai's Redevelopment of the West Bund Pushes Out Art Galleries" (19 July 2024): art spaces including ShanghArt, Don Gallery, Aike Gallery, Pond Society, Qiao Space and Ding Yi's studio were displaced in a large-scale redevelopment of the district, which the article describes as shifting toward technology and finance.

The July article says aspirations for "a dynamic, enduring new cultural enclave" now appear "ever more improbable". It lists TANK Shanghai among the private museums the district attracted and does not report TANK as displaced.
Qiao Space, Qiao's other gallery, shut on 15 June 2024 and was demolished; TANK stands on the same waterfront, which the West Bund Development Group manages (The Art Newspaper, 2019).

press_items.title: Lisa Movius, "Collector Qiao Zhibing's delayed Tank Shanghai museum opens on West Bund waterfront" (2019)
Tina Shan, "In Shanghai, Carving Out a Space for Critiques of Consumerism" (2019)

name: Lugar a Dudas
overview: Artist-run, self-managed non-profit art space in the Granada neighbourhood of Cali (Helguera, 2024; MoMA's Post, 2017). Its programme: a library specialised in contemporary art, residencies, a cinema club, exhibitions, talks and the online project Secuela.

Founded in 2005 by the artist Oscar Muñoz, who still directs it (MoMA's Post, 2017; Pablo Helguera, 2024). A directory lists 2006. The space's own history page says it has worked since 2005. The history page does not name the founders.
The name is Spanish and means "place for doubts" (my translation).
funding_verdict: Lugar a Dudas: foundation-funded, now running on savings and its own resources
wider_context: The Art Newspaper (Melanie Gerlis, 31 May 2013): a Turin appeals court sentenced Stephan Schmidheiny, head of the Eternit group, to 18 years over the deaths of 3,000 people exposed to asbestos since 1976; he denied the charges and was appealing. It also reported that Schmidheiny's estranged wife owned 70% of the autonomous Daros LatinAmerica collection. The piece does not mention Lugar a Dudas.

Daros Latin America supported the launch of Lugar a Dudas in 2005 and is credited among past funders; no reporting found of Daros money reaching the space today. Wikipedia reports the Daros Latinamerica Collection was acquired in its entirety by MALBA, announced in December 2025.

press_items.title: Pablo Helguera, "La Gran Vitrina / The Great Vitrine" (2024)
Marta Dansie, "Growing Seeds of Thought: 10 Days in Colombia" (2017)

name: Casa Tres Patios (C3P)
overview: House at Carrera 50A #63-31 in the Prado neighbourhood of Medellín. The site describes the Fundación Casa Tres Patios as a non-profit organisation dedicated to promoting social justice.
Global Voices (2014) says the house was founded by Tony Evanko and has offered artists and local communities a space since 2006. The foundation's own history page gives 2007 as its start.
A 2012 shift moved the programme toward critical thinking and education for social justice, and after 2018 it introduced the Laboratorios Comunes de Creación, a pedagogical model (C3P history page).
funding_verdict: Casa Tres Patios: designated donations from the Foundation For Arts Initiative, Fundación Sofía Pérez de Soto, Fundación SURA and Arts Collaboratory, research service fees and an annual art auction

name: TEOR/éTica
overview: Independent, private, non-profit project for art and thought at Calle 7 Av. 11, Carmen, San José, with an emphasis on contemporary art of Central America and the Caribbean (stated by the space).

Founded in 1999 on the initiative of the artist, curator and researcher Virginia Pérez-Ratton (1950 to 2010). The founding assembly was Rolando Castellón, Paulo Herkenhoff, Claude Tournon and Bruno Stagno (stated by the space).

Pérez-Ratton was the first director of the Museum of Contemporary Art and Design (MADC) in San José from 1994 to 1998, received the Prince Claus Award in 2002 and Costa Rica's Magón National Prize for Culture in 2009, and died on 6 October 2010 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: TEOR/éTica: private non-profit, with international arts-network collaborators

name: MMSU, Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Rijeka
aliases: Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Rijeka
overview: MMSU is at Krešimirova 26c, Rijeka (museum website).
The pages read gave no founding year or building history.

What is there: the January to June 2024 report names painting, photography and poster collections and the B. Rašica collection, and shows a year of shows built from the fund; the pages read gave no total object count (MMSU half-year report 2024).
funding_verdict: MMSU: public, City of Rijeka plus Ministry of Culture
